current_description_proposal.description_long:
An Associated Press report published in April 2017 said U.S. imports of Ivanka Trump merchandise had risen an estimated 166% over the prior year, with almost all of the goods coming from China. The report also said sales for the brand had reached record levels. The 166% figure concerns imports; it is not a reported increase in profits or sales. That distinction is important because the original claim overstated what the statistic showed.

The business reporting also described provisional Chinese trademark approvals for Ivanka Trump's company while she was serving in the White House. The import growth and the trademark approvals are related to the public scrutiny around the brand, but they are separate developments and should not be collapsed into one claim. The supplied information does not establish that the trademark approvals caused the rise in imports, nor does it quantify the brand's profits. It does establish that the business was experiencing record sales while imports rose sharply and that its company received provisional trademark approvals in China during Ivanka Trump's White House service.

Together, those facts help explain why the brand raised conflict-of-interest concerns. They do not, on their own, prove that government actions produced the commercial results or that any law was violated. The supported account is narrower: the brand had substantial commercial activity, merchandise imports were overwhelmingly from China, and the company received provisional trademark approvals during her time in the White House.

The State Department began requesting social-media identifiers from most immigrant and nonimmigrant visa applicants worldwide in 2019, following earlier screening directives. In June 2025, as student and exchange-visitor visa appointments resumed, the department added more comprehensive online-presence review for applicants in the F, M, and J categories and asked them to make their social-media accounts public for review. Those are separate policies with different scopes and dates. The supplied correction rejects the claim that Trump signed a January 2025 order requiring every applicant to provide five years of social-media history or face denial for political speech; the linked records do not support that description. The documented expansion concerns review of students’ online presence, while the older identifier collection was broader. The distinction is important for describing who was affected and when. This account does not claim that every applicant was denied or that any particular person’s political views determined a visa decision.

The companies described plans to invest up to $500 billion in the United States over four years, with an initial $100 billion commitment. The project was a private-sector venture rather than an executive order, and the headline figure described prospective investment rather than money already spent. Stargate drew attention to the scale of data-center construction and the central role large technology companies expected to play in expanding U.S. computing capacity. The supplied correction rejects a claim that SoftBank received favorable regulatory treatment in exchange for its pledge; the announcement does not establish such a bargain. Trump’s participation gave the venture political prominence, but the investment plan remained dependent on the companies’ future decisions and project execution. The announcement marked a commitment to build AI infrastructure, not evidence that every planned dollar had been deployed or that the government had approved a specific regulatory exchange.
